description: What each SCALAR operator of esm-spec §9.2's evaluable core COMPUTES, pinned once for every binding. The op vocabulary is named in the spec and its tiers are gated by the registry corpus, but nothing shared said what `sign(0)`, `7/2`, `atan2(y, x)` or a false comparison is WORTH — each binding pinned it privately, against its own evaluator, in its own vocabulary: Julia through `build_evaluator` on hand-built AST nodes (tree_walk_test.jl), Rust through `interpret()` on a `ResolvedExpr` tree (interpret.rs), Python through `_expr_to_sympy` unit tests (test_simulation_scalar_ops.py). Three private op tables and no cross-binding gate is exactly the shape in which two bindings disagree for a year. The fixture is ALGEBRAIC: every operator is an observed whose operands are declared PARAMETERS, asserted at a single static evaluation (CONFORMANCE_SPEC §5.43), so no integrator stands between the operator and the number and the band is the arithmetic's alone. A second test re-asserts a subset under `parameter_overrides`, so a binding that folded the declared defaults at build time and ignored the overrides lands on the first test's numbers and fails.

scope_excluded.go: No simulator and no inline-test runner, so a tier that DRIVES one cannot be run here (API_SPEC.md §3, capability profiles). This is an exclusion from the CATEGORY, not from the rule.
scope_excluded.typescript: No simulator and no inline-test runner, so a tier that DRIVES one cannot be run here (API_SPEC.md §3, capability profiles). This is an exclusion from the CATEGORY, not from the rule.

tolerances.detail: §5.38.2's `algebraic` class. These are single evaluations of scalar arithmetic, so two correct bindings differ only in the last bits of a transcendental; nothing here carries an integrator's error except the one `probe` assertion, which declares its own looser band in the document.

fixtures.note: Authored here. Migrated from tree_walk_test.jl testsets 1-5, interpret.rs and test_simulation_scalar_ops.py.
Authored here, SPLIT OUT of `scalar_operator_semantics` because it is the one core operator the three bindings do not agree on.

named_exclusions.reason: Julia's tree-walk evaluator carries an evaluation rule for the `true` literal op and NONE for `false`, so the build refuses this document with `unevaluable_operator`: "operator 'false' is an evaluable-core op with no evaluation rule in the tree-walk evaluator". Measured 2026-09-22 on compiler/testmig at 25efca83a, under both `interpreter` and `native`.

Rust classes `false` as a REWRITE TARGET and refuses it before evaluation with `unlowered_operator`: "rewrite-target operator 'false' reached evaluation without being lowered to a stencil by a rewrite rule". Only Python answers this operator today. Measured 2026-09-22 on compiler/testmig at 25efca83a, under both `interpreter` and `native`.

fixtures.golden_absent_reason: The REFERENCE itself refuses this document: the Julia `interpreter` has no evaluation rule for the `false` op, so there is no reference actual to mint and `--write-golden` skips it. The fixture is NOT ungated — Python, the one binding that answers `false` today, is still held to the DOCUMENT's own `expected` values (`false == 0`, and the state it drives reaching 0 at t = 1), which is an oracle outside every binding. What is missing is the cross-compiler drift check, and it comes back the moment Julia gains the rule and the golden can be minted.

fixtures.note: Authored here, SPLIT OUT of `scalar_operator_semantics` because Rust refuses the `pow` spelling that Julia and Python evaluate.

named_exclusions.reason: Rust classes `pow` as a REWRITE TARGET rather than an evaluable-core operator and refuses it before evaluation with `unlowered_operator`: "rewrite-target operator 'pow' reached evaluation without being lowered to a stencil by a rewrite rule". Julia and Python both evaluate it, and both give the same number as `^`, which the sibling fixture pins under the caret spelling. Measured 2026-09-22 on compiler/testmig at 25efca83a, under both `interpreter` and `native` — so this is not a `native` strictness question but a disagreement about what the core vocabulary IS.

fixtures.note: Authored here, SPLIT OUT of `scalar_operator_semantics` because Rust's strict `native` has no wholesale lowering for the `true` leaf.

named_exclusions.reason: Rust's strict `native` has no wholesale lowering for the `true` literal op: “compiler 'native' cannot run the const-cadence observed 'literal_true': wholesale: unsupported op `true`”. Rust's `interpreter` runs it, and Julia and Python run it under both compilers, so this is a `native` coverage gap on ONE leaf rather than a disagreement about the vocabulary — unlike `pow` and `false`, which Rust refuses under `interpreter` too. Measured 2026-09-22 on compiler/testmig at 25efca83a.
